t: prohibitory vows. Vows by which a person forbids to himself things that are permitted to him (Hilchot Nedarim 1:1).
to eat things the verse forbade to him from the grapevine. As detailed below, 5:1-2.
he receives two sets of lashes. Two lashing punishments (each of which is thirty-nine lashes).
one because of "he shall not profane his word," which includes all vows. The negative commandment that a person not profane his vow, which exists in every vow (Hilchot Nedarim 1:5).

and one because of a matter among the things forbidden, with a special prohibition on the nazir. For he incurs a separate lashing punishment for each of the forbidden things a nazir does (see below 5:8).
one, "he shall do according to all that came out of his mouth". That is a positive commandment in every vow (Hilchot Nedarim 1:4).
his shaving along with bringing his offerings. For there is a mitzvah to shave and bring offerings at the end of his nazirite term (see below 8:1).

he is a nazir immediately, lest he die now. Although his nazirite term does not take effect immediately, since he did not set a defined time for it, he must begin to observe nezirut immediately out of concern that he may die.

and if after his nezirut, he transgresses "do not delay to fulfill it". For whoever makes a vow must fulfill it immediately when he is able (see Hilchot Matnot Aniyim 8:1; and unlike the law of "do not delay" regarding bringing offerings, which he transgresses only after three festivals have passed, as explained in Hilchot Ma'aseh ha-Korbanot 14:13).

and one does not receive lashes for this negative commandment. Because it involves no action, and one does not receive lashes for any negative commandment that involves no action (see also Hilchot Ma'aseh ha-Korbanot, there).

we do not say that in nezirut ... until he expresses it with his lips etc.. For nezirut it suffices that he decide in his mind to be a nazir and that he utter a statement that can be interpreted as accepting nezirut, even if he does not say so explicitly.
I will be "naveh". I will be beautiful, that is, in growing hair.
"mekhalkel". An expression that denotes growing and multiplying hair.
"mesalsel". An expression that denotes tending to the hair.
to let the locks grow. To grow the hair.
if he said, "I take upon myself birds..." he is not a nazir. Because bringing birds is not an act unique to a nazir, since one can bring them as a voluntary offering.
and he is like one who did not utter anything with his lips. He obligated himself neither in nezirut nor in bringing birds to the Temple.

places of stammerers who alter speech. For stammerers among the nations of the world who lived near Jews would distort the words of the Hebrew language, and gradually these words would penetrate even the common speech of the Jews in that place (Commentary on the Mishnah, Nazir 1:1; and see also Hilchot Shevuot 2:5, Hilchot Nedarim 1:16).
the seeds. The inner pits of the grape.
the skins. The outer peels of the grape.
dried figs. Dried figs.
pressed figs. Figs stuck together.
he is forbidden these. For his words are interpreted as a vow to forbid himself these things.
and he is not a nazir. Although he said the word "nazir," since these things are not forbidden to a nazir.
bitter of soul. And because of bitterness he does not want wine.
to satiate him. To give him drink to satiety.

to the drunkenness of Lot. That he is not aware of his actions, like Lot, who did not know his actions in his drunkenness (Genesis 19:30-35; for further implications see Hilchot Ishut 4:18, Hilchot Gerushin 2:14, Hilchot Mechirah 29:18).
and anyone who stipulates against what is written in the Torah, his stipulation is void. For a person cannot exempt himself from what the Torah obligates him (Hilchot Ishut 6:9).
and we have already explained. Above 5:9.
because I bury the dead. And therefore he thought it would be permitted for him to become impure for a corpse.
vows made in error, which do not require inquiry of a sage, as we explained. Hilchot Nedarim 4:1-2; a vow made by mistake is not binding and does not need to be released with the help of a sage.

any limb which, if removed from a living person, he would die; if he said, "This is a nazir," he is a nazir. Since a person's life depends on it, it is considered as representing the whole person (see also Hilchot Arachin va-Charamin 2:1).
a tumtum. One whose sexual organs are covered and it is not apparent whether he is male or female. [Note: in his Commentary on the Mishnah the Rambam vocalizes this word "tumtum."]
and an androgynos. One who has both male and female organs, and the Sages did not decide whether he is treated as male or female (Hilchot Ishut 2:24).
unintentionally. That at the time of his nezirut he did not know the laws of nezirut and their meaning (see above 1:15; and see also Hilchot Shevuot 3:5-6, Hilchot Nedarim 8:3).
under coercion. That he was forced to vow nezirut (see also Hilchot Shevuot 3:1, Hilchot Nedarim 4:1).
to urge his fellow. To persuade him to do a certain thing (Hilchot Nedarim 4:3).
by way of exaggeration. Hyperbole (Hilchot Shevuot 3:5).
and regretted. Changed his mind.
just as other vows are released. For the laws of releasing vows see Hilchot Shevuot 6:1-6, Hilchot Nedarim 4:5.

and went to bring his offerings, having taken the nazirite vow with the intention of bringing them when his vow days are complete. For when he took the nazirite vow he intended to bring certain animals that were in his possession.
one who attaches himself to nezirut. One who obligates himself in nezirut on the strength of another's nezirut.
as we explained regarding the law of anyone who attaches himself to a vow. Hilchot Nedarim 3:3.
"The pressing of my hands from wine... my hair, from being cut," he is a nazir. And since he forbade himself one of the nazirite prohibitions, he is forbidden in all of them (above 1:9).
within the time of a statement. Within the time it takes to say the words "Shalom aleikha, Rabbi" after the first one's statement (Hilchot Shevuot 2:17).
his fellow is a nazir immediately. And his acceptance of nezirut does not depend on his having a son like the first, since we interpret that he intended the nezirut itself without the condition.
and his fellow heard. A third person who was present.
that I would like you to have a son like this one. That I want you to have a son like this friend, who took a nazirite vow.
for he is embarrassed before him. So that his fellow will not think he does not want him to have a son. And since he did so only out of embarrassment, his intention was not for nezirut.
perhaps he intended only to be a nazir like him. For the friend in question is not present, so we cannot say that he said so out of embarrassment.
and a doubtful nezirut is treated leniently. And therefore he is not a nazir (unlike vows, in which we are stringent in cases of doubt - Hilchot Nedarim 9:4).
neither of them is a nazir. For it is a doubt, and a doubtful nezirut is treated leniently.
in a pile. A heap of grain.
kor. A measure of volume.

the koy. An animal resembling both a goat and a deer, about which the Sages did not decide whether it belongs to the species of wild animals or the species of domesticated animals (Commentary on the Mishnah, Bikkurim 2:8).
androgynos. See above 1:17 for explanation.
and all these differences are in matters of the mitzvah, not in its nature and make-up. These differences are halachic in significance, not biological and physical.
its blood requires covering like a wild animal. As opposed to the blood of a slaughtered domesticated animal, which does not require covering with earth after slaughter (Hilchot Shechitah 14:4).
and its fat is forbidden like that of a domesticated animal. As opposed to the fat of a wild animal, which is not forbidden to eat (Hilchot Ma'achalot Asurot 1:13).
a mixed-breed with both a domesticated animal and a wild animal. That it is forbidden to crossbreed it with either a wild or a domesticated animal (Hilchot Kilayim 9:5).

and each of them will be explained in its place. For example the prohibition of slaughtering it on a festival, or covering its blood (Hilchot Yom Tov 3:1), and the obligation to bring the priestly gifts from it (Hilchot Bikkurim 9:5), and more.
he conveys impurity through white, like men. Like a ba'al keri or a zav, who convey impurity through semen, whose color is white (Hilchot Metam'ei Mishkav u'Moshav 1:6).
and through red, like women. Like a niddah or a zavah, who convey impurity through blood, whose color is red (there).

and he is not sold as a Hebrew slave, neither like men nor like women. A man is sold for his theft and also sells himself as a Hebrew slave, which is not the case for a woman (Hilchot Avadim 1:2), whereas a minor daughter is sold by her father, unlike a son, who is not sold by his father (Hilchot Avadim 4:1). The androgynos is a doubt and is not sold at all.
and one who kills him is executed for it. Like the law of one who intentionally kills a Jew (Hilchot Rotzeach 1:1).

and each of them will be explained in its place. For example that his wife is exempt from chalitzah and yibbum (Hilchot Yibbum va-Chalitzah 6:8), and that he is forbidden to be secluded with women (Hilchot Issurei Bi'ah 22:11), and that he is disqualified from testifying (Hilchot Edut 9:3), and more.
sighted. Seeing, with open eyes.
blind. Unable to see.
all of them are nazirites. For everyone's words are correct (at least partially).

a minor who has reached the age of vows. A boy from the age of thirteen years and a day, and a girl from the age of twelve years and a day. From this age they are obligated to fulfill their vows (see Hilchot Nedarim 11:1-4; and although it is explained there that even before then their vows can have validity, the law is not so regarding nezirut - see Igrot Moshe, Even ha-Ezer 1:170).

even though he has not yet grown two hairs. Which are the signs of adulthood for male and female (see Hilchot Ishut chapter 2), and in other matters their acts have no halachic validity without these signs.
a halachah received by tradition. A halachic tradition.
and the father is obligated to have him observe all the details of nezirut. To see to it that the son observes all the laws of the nazir.
and if he becomes impure he brings the offering of impurity. Like the law of any nazir who became impure (see below 6:3).
he brings the offering of purity. Which the nazir must bring at the end of his nazirite days (below 8:1).
until he grows up and becomes a man. Until he reaches the age of thirteen years and one day and grows two hairs in the pubic region (Hilchot Ishut 2:10).
the son did not want. To accept nezirut through his father.
and protested. Expressed opposition.
as it says, "Speak to the children of Israel". And the continuation of the verse is: "and say to them: a man or a woman who makes a special vow, the vow of a nazir."
and a father or a husband may annul a woman's nezirut. For the details of the conditions for annulment by a father and husband see Hilchot Nedarim 11:6 onward.

a slave: his master may compel him to drink and to become impure for the dead. For it says about the nazir, "for the consecration of his God is upon his head," from which it follows that he must be subject only to his God, whereas the slave is under his master's authority (Aruch ha-Shulchan, based on the Yerushalmi).
that involve self-affliction. That weaken the slave's body.
or who pledged the valuation. Who vowed his value to the Temple, and is obligated to give the amount set in the Torah (Hilchot Arachin va-Charamin 1:1-2).
because his person is not acquired by himself, the vow does not take effect on him. Compare Hilchot Shevuot 12:6.
for a slave is compelled and not annulled for. The way a slave's vow is canceled by the master is through compulsion and not through annulment.
and if he annulled it for him, he goes free. Like any act done by a master to his slave in a way that is normally done only to a free person, through which the slave goes free (Hilchot Avadim 8:17).

a slave who vowed nezirut and fled, or whose master went etc.. Although the slave is not with his master, he is still considered to be in his domain, and therefore his permission to drink depends on his master's compelling him. In this case there is no compulsion from the master, since the master wants him not to drink wine now so that the slave will suffer and want to return to him so that he will compel him to drink.

he took the vow, completed his nezirut and shaved, and his master did not know... he has fulfilled his vow. Although it is possible that had his master found out he would have compelled him and canceled the nezirut, since in fact his master did not find out and did not compel him, he has fulfilled his obligation of nezirut.

but if he vowed and did not shave and went free, he has not fulfilled his vow. Since while under his master it is possible that his master would compel him to cancel his nezirut, even if he observed nezirut in practice it does not count, and when he is freed he must count the days of his nezirut from the beginning (Chazon Devorah on the Tosefta, end of Nazir).

if he became impure and afterward went free, he counts from the time he became impure. When he became impure while still a slave and was freed after he began counting his seven days of impurity, he does not need to count his days of impurity again. For although the days of nezirut do not count for a slave who is under his master, nevertheless the days of impurity do count for him (Chazon Devorah).
in the presence of the Temple. When the Temple exists.
because we have no Temple etc.. And the nezirut ends only with shaving and bringing offerings.

nezirut applies only in the Land of Israel. Although by basic law the nazirite vow takes effect outside the Land, in practice it is impossible to observe nezirut there, since the Sages decreed corpse impurity on one who is outside the Land ("impurity of the land of the nations" - see Hilchot Tum'at Met chapter 11), and therefore nezirut cannot be observed there.
plain nezirut. Without specifying a time.

"I am a nazir with a very, very great nezirut, a great deal" etc.. We interpret his intention as being that the nezirut is very hard for him and as if lasting a long time (Commentary on the Mishnah, Nazir 1:3, based on the Babylonian Talmud).
from the tradition. A halachic tradition.

for one cannot vow hours. From the verse "the days of his nazirite vow" (Numbers 6:4) it is learned that one does not vow hours, and an hour is counted as a full day (Commentary on the Mishnah, Nazir 1:3).
he set out on the road. He began walking on that road.
for he intended only a long nezirut. And since he did not specify its time, he is a nazir for thirty days (as above, halachah 1).
and if he set out on the road etc.. Since he began walking on it, his intention was for the time of walking this road.
he is a nazir according to the number he said. Separate nezirut terms of thirty days each.
he shaves and brings his offerings. Like any nazir who completes his nezirut (below 8:1).

he counts his nezirut terms according to the number of days of the year. This does not mean that he accepted one nezirut that would continue for all the days of the year, but that he accepted separate nezirut terms according to the number of days of the year, each one of thirty days like plain nezirut.
a solar year. One revolution of the earth around the sun.
a lunar year. Twelve lunar months, and the difference between a lunar year and a solar year is about eleven days (see Hilchot Kiddush ha-Chodesh 6:4).
and if he did not specify. He did not explain his words.
for we have explained. Hilchot Nedarim 9:1.
"I am a nazir one and a half," he is a nazir twice. For there is no nezirut of less than thirty days, and even his saying "and a half" is a nezirut of thirty days.
"I am a nazir and one day". This implies one plain nezirut and another nezirut of one day, and there is no nezirut shorter than thirty days.

"I am a nazir and one hour," he is a nazir twice. For this implies one plain nezirut and another nezirut of one hour, and an hour is counted as a day, and there is no nezirut shorter than thirty days. Whereas had he said, "I am a nazir for thirty days and one hour," he would be a nazir for thirty-one days (as above, halachah 4).
groups. Sets.
and all of them testify to two. And on this point there is no contradiction among them.
and he counted the first and set aside an offering. He finished counting the first nezirut and set aside the offerings he must bring at the end of his nezirut.
the first counted for him toward the second. The first nezirut is considered for him as fulfilling the second nezirut, and he need not observe additional nezirut himself.
and even if he brought his atonement. That not only did he set aside his offerings but he had already offered them before he was asked about the first nezirut.
and even if he shaved his hair. As a nazir does after offering his sacrifices (below 8:2).
for the second takes effect only after the first. And since there is a connection between the two nezirut terms, the days of the first nezirut can count toward the second.
and the first, once he released it, it is as if it does not uproot it. And therefore the second nezirut takes effect in its place.
until the fulfillment of their days. Until all the days of his nezirut are complete.
he shaves with a razor. He shaves.
the offerings of three animals when he shaves. Like the law of a nazir who completes his nazirite days (below 8:1).

as it says, "And it was at the end of days that he would shave it, for it was heavy upon him, and he shaved it". The verse speaks of Avshalom, son of King David, who would shave his hair every year ("at the end of days"), and the Sages had a tradition that he was a nazir for life (Commentary on the Mishnah, Nazir 1:2).
Shimshon. Shimshon ben Manoach, who was one of the judges of Israel (Judges chapters 13-16).

the angel separated him from impurity. The angel who appeared to his parents commanded them that his mother be careful not to eat or drink things forbidden to a nazir ("anything impure" - Babylonian Talmud, Sotah 9b), and to set Shimshon apart for nezirut, as it says: "You shall conceive and bear a son; now beware and do not drink wine or strong drink and do not eat anything impure, for behold, you will conceive and bear a son, and no razor shall come upon his head, for the child shall be a nazir of God from the womb" (Judges 13:3-5).
he cannot be released from his vow. To go to a sage to annul this nazirite vow.
like the husband of Delilah. See Judges 16:4.
like one who uprooted the doors of Gaza. When the people of Gaza lay in ambush to kill him (there 16:3).
like one whose eyes the Philistines gouged out. After Delilah shaved his hair and they seized him (there 16:19-21).

Shmuel of Ramah. The prophet Shmuel, son of Chanah and Elkanah, who lived in Ramah. Before he was born, Chanah vowed that the son born to her would be a lifelong nazir, as it says: "And I will give him to God all the days of his life, and no razor shall come upon his head" (I Samuel 1:11; and see Mishnah Nazir 9:5).
like one who hacked Agag to pieces at Gilgal. After the war with Amalek, Shmuel cut Agag, king of Amalek, to pieces with a sword at the place called Gilgal (I Samuel 15:33).
the basket. A box, a chest.
if he said, "It was not my intention to be a nazir all my days... " he is a nazir for thirty days only. As above, halachah 1.
we view the basket as if it were full of mustard seeds. We assume that his intention was to take a nazirite vow for a number of days equal to the mustard seeds that fill the house or the basket.

and he may shave from twelve months to twelve months... like other lifelong nazirites. This is not like one who vowed nezirut for a thousand years (above, halachah 11), because here there is no set time.

this is like one who said, "I take upon myself nezirut according to the number of the hairs of my head" etc.. Because the hairs or the grains of dust and sand are separate from one another, we interpret his intention as separate nezirut terms one after another. This is unlike the contents of the house or basket in the previous halachah, which are one thing, and therefore we interpret his words as a count of nazirite days (based on the Commentary on the Mishnah, Nazir 1:4).
and at each shaving he does not drink wine or become impure for the dead. For there is no interruption between the nezirut terms, and immediately at the end of one he is obligated in the next.
one who says, "I am a nazir". And he is obligated in nezirut for thirty days (above 3:1).

he shaves the shaving of purity. "The shaving of purity" is a term for the nazir's acts at the end of his nezirut, namely bringing his offerings and shaving his hair (Commentary on the Mishnah, Nazir 3:2).
and if he shaved on the thirtieth day, he has fulfilled it. For part of the thirtieth day counts for him as a full day.
he said, "I am a nazir for thirty days," he shaves only on the thirty-first day. When he explicitly said "thirty days," we say that he took upon himself thirty complete days.

and the second on the sixty-first day. And the thirty-first day on which he shaved for his first nezirut also counts for him as the first day of the second nezirut, so he shaves for the second nezirut too on the sixty-first day.

he completes his own and afterward counts his son's. He finishes the days of nezirut, shaves and brings his offerings, and afterward begins the nezirut for his son, because in taking on the nezirut he put his own nezirut before his son's.

he interrupts his own nezirut and counts his son's. Since in taking on the nezirut he put his son's nezirut first, when the son is born he must stop his nezirut without bringing offerings and begin to count the days of his son's nezirut. And when he finishes it, he shaves and brings offerings for this nezirut.
and afterward he returns and completes his own. And at the end of his nezirut he shaves and brings offerings for his nezirut.
and both are like one nezirut. The first days of his nezirut and his son's nezirut are considered one nezirut.
therefore, if he became impure during his son's nezirut, he voids everything. Even the days of his nezirut that he began beforehand, since it is considered part of his son's nezirut.

if he became impure after his son's nezirut, when he began to complete his nezirut, he voids only up to his son's nezirut. Only the days of his nezirut after his son's nezirut, for there is no connection between the earlier and later days of his nezirut except for the count of days.

and it turns out he loses from before the birth ten days, from day seventy to the birth. For he must observe thirty days of nezirut and not twenty, and he lost every day on which he observed nezirut beyond the seventy days, since he will have to observe thirty days of nezirut again afterward.
one who says, "I am a nazir after twenty days". By this statement he obligated himself after twenty days to observe thirty days of nezirut, like plain nezirut.

he does not shave for this nezirut that he vowed last. Since the Shimshon-type nezirut took effect on him after twenty days, he can no longer shave for the first nezirut (and see the commentators on the Rambam, who discussed the reason for this).
he is forbidden to drink wine, to become impure and to shave forever. For a person does not know when the day of his death will be, and we are concerned that he may die tomorrow (see also above 1:4).
if he vowed on a weekday, he is forbidden forever. Lest the day come.

for it is a doubt whether he will come on Shabbat or a festival or will not come. For the Sages were uncertain whether the son of David can come on Shabbatot and festivals (see Babylonian Talmud, Eruvin 43b).

and the coming Shabbat, which is a doubt, does not nullify a nezirut that already took effect. Since he already began to observe his nezirut, he observes his nezirut even on the coming Shabbatot, although for them too there is a doubt whether he will come or not.
he is forbidden to shave, to drink wine and to become impure for the dead. And he is permitted in all of them after he brings his offerings, even if he has not yet shaved his head (see below 8:5).
he counts from the time he vowed. By Torah law, although he did not observe his vow, because drinking wine does not void the nezirut (as below 6:1).

that he observe prohibition for as many days as he observed permissibility. That he add to the days of his nezirut the number of days on which he behaved as permitted (Commentary on the Mishnah, Nazir 5:3).
they give him makat mardut. Rabbinic lashes.
in a short nezirut. Of only thirty days.
in a long nezirut. Which is more than thirty days.
it suffices that he observe thirty days of nezirut. The Sages did not punish him with more than thirty days.
even though he violated his long nezirut for all its days. For example, if he vowed a hundred days and behaved as permitted for all of them.
and if he did not observe the prohibition himself. If he did not begin to observe nezirut for the number of days he behaved as permitted in a short nezirut, or for thirty days in a long nezirut.
we do not attend to him at all. If he comes to ask for release from his nezirut, they do not release it for him.
or they will open an opening for them. To find a reason to release their vow and nezirut.

he cannot annul. For after the blood was thrown he was permitted to drink wine (below 8:5), and this is not a vow of self-affliction that a husband has permission to annul for his wife (Hilchot Nedarim 12:1).
in the shaving of purity. That the nazir brings at the end of his nezirut, after which there is no further shaving.
but in the shaving of impurity. That the nazir brings when he became impure, after which shaving he must observe his nezirut again and shave at its end.
because she still needs to count another nezirut. And he can annul for her in order to release her to drink wine.
types. Kinds of prohibitions.
the impurity. The prohibition of becoming impure for the dead.
and the shaving. To cut the hair of his head.
the strong drink. Intoxicating beverage.
dried figs. Dried figs.
and this strong drink that was forbidden to him in the Torah. As it says: "He shall abstain from wine and strong drink; he shall not drink vinegar of wine or vinegar of strong drink" (Numbers 6:3).
the strong drink of a wine mixture. Strong drink that is mainly wine (Sefer ha-Mitzvot, Negative Commandment 202, and see Aruch ha-Shulchan 13:6, who brings further explanations there).
unripe grapes. Unripe fruit.
the inner ones that are planted. The inner seeds of the grape that can be planted in the ground.
an olive-bulk of congealed wine. Dried wine, which is considered food, and therefore its measure is an olive-bulk.
and the tendrils. The blossoms at the tips of the branches while still tender.
and vine water. Water that drips from the tree if it is cut or wounded.
and the semadar. The bud of the vine from which the grape grows (Commentary on the Mishnah, Orlah 1:7).

all the grapevine prohibitions combine with one another. Although the grapevine prohibitions are divided into separate prohibitions (as in halachah 8 below), if he ate from them together a quantity of an olive-bulk, he receives lashes (unlike other food prohibitions, which do not combine with one another - Hilchot Ma'achalot Asurot 4:16).

until the forbidden thing in a mixture is an olive-bulk within the time of eating three eggs. For one who eats a mixture does not receive lashes unless the mixture contains the measure of an olive-bulk of the forbidden substance for every three eggs of permitted substance.
like other prohibitions that are equal for everyone. In this law the nazirite prohibitions are no different from other food prohibitions.
as we explained in Hilchot Ma'achalot Asurot. 14:8.

a revi'it of wine within the time of eating a peras. A peras is half a loaf of bread, whose measure is three eggs, and one is not liable for lashes until there is a revi'it of wine for every three eggs.
grape soak. Something soaked in liquid that came from grapes.
its taste. The taste of the mixture.
and its substance. The measure within the time of eating a peras, which is a substantive measure.
like other forbidden foods. For only when the mixture has both taste and substance is there a Torah prohibition (Hilchot Ma'achalot Asurot 15:2).
this should not be more severe than fat and blood. Which are forbidden by Torah law to eat, but are permitted when their mixtures have no taste (Hilchot Ma'achalot Asurot 15:2).
as we explained regarding forbidden foods. 15:2, that a mixture of a forbidden substance that has taste without substance is forbidden to eat by rabbinic law.
makat mardut. Rabbinic lashes.
even if he squeezed a cluster and drank a revi'it from it. Before the juice fermented, nevertheless it is called wine and he receives lashes for drinking it.
because of "he shall not profane his word," which is the same in all vows. For one who violates his vow transgresses this negative commandment (above 1:2, Hilchot Nedarim 1:5).
for it does not say "wine he shall not drink" and vinegar etc.. It turns out that the verse does not have a separate negative commandment for wine and one for vinegar.

rather it says, "vinegar of wine and vinegar of strong drink he shall not drink" etc.. From this it follows that the "vinegar" in the verse does not come as a beverage standing on its own, but as part of the description of the wine or strong drink, and "vinegar" is not stated here as an additional negative commandment, but to teach us that even when the wine or strong drink turned sour, the prohibition of drinking did not leave them (see Sefer ha-Mitzvot, Negative Commandment 206).

since it repeated only the vinegar, which is one name, he does not receive lashes for this separately and for that separately. Therefore he does not receive lashes twice for wine vinegar and strong drink vinegar (see Radbaz).
although he is liable by Heaven for each and every revi'it. For with each drinking of a revi'it he transgresses a Torah prohibition.
as we explained. Above, halachah 8.
and if they warned him for each and every revi'it... he is liable for each one. See also Hilchot Ma'achalot Asurot 14:7.
by rabbinic law. By the words of the Sages.
to stand in the company of wine drinkers. To stay at the place of a wine party.
with a razor. With a shaving blade.
with scissors. With a pair of scissors.
he cut it from its root in the manner of a razor. He cut the hair from its root attached to the skin.

whether the shaver or the one being shaved, as it says, "a razor shall not pass over his head". And since it is written "shall not pass" and not "shall not cause to pass," this implies that the prohibition is not specifically on the nazir, but that it is forbidden for a razor to pass over his head, regardless of who passes it.
long enough to bend its tip to its root. A length sufficient to bend the end of the hair to its root.
a substance that makes the hair fall out. An ointment or liquid that causes hair to fall out.
he does not receive lashes. Because this is not in the manner of a razor.
with a powder. With a powder that makes the hair fall out.
and if he did so, he does not receive lashes. For it is not in the manner of a razor.
seven-day impurity. Impurity that lasts seven days.
both for impurities for which he shaves. For some corpse impurities, the nazir voids his nezirut, brings impurity offerings, shaves and begins counting his nezirut anew.
as will be explained. Below 7:1-2.

and for impurities for which he does not shave. For other impurities he must wait until he becomes pure, but he does not void his days of nezirut and does not bring offerings and shave (as below 7:6).
if he became impure and separated. After he became impure, he separated himself from the impurity he had become impure with, and afterward he again made himself impure with another impurity.
and he touched, carried, or formed a tent again. That he became impure through a corpse in one of these ways.
for he is already in a state of defilement. Since he did not separate from the impurity, there is no new act of defilement here, so he does not receive lashes.

a chest, box, or tower. Vessels that, if their volume exceeds forty se'ah, do not receive impurity (see Hilchot Kelim 3:2). When their lid is sealed, what is inside them does not become impure (see Hilchot Tum'at Met 21:1).

and he removed the roof of the chest above him with his knowledge. The nazirite deliberately opened the lid of the vessel, and now the nazirite is under one roof with the corpse and becomes impure through a tent.
one for "he shall not come". "He shall not come near a dead body" (Numbers 6:6), which teaches that it is forbidden to enter the tent of a corpse.
and one for "he shall not defile himself". This is the prohibition against becoming impure through a corpse.
for impurity and entering occur together. Since he violated both prohibitions at once, he receives lashes for both.

But if he entered in the usual way, his impurity precedes his entering. Just as he is not liable for further impurity when he did not separate from the earlier one (as explained in the previous halakhah), so he is not liable for his entering once he was already defiled (compare Hilchot Evel 3:6-7).
provided that he stays there for the time of a prostration. The length of time of a prostration, lying flat on the ground (for the definition of the measure see Hilchot Bi'at Mikdash 3:23).

like an impure person who entered the Temple. A person who entered the Temple while pure and became impure must leave immediately; if he stayed there for the time of a prostration, he is liable (ibid. 21-22).

and the one who defiled him transgresses "you shall not place a stumbling block before the blind". Whoever strengthens the hands of transgressors or causes them to stumble violates this prohibition (Hilchot Rotze'ach 12:14). But one does not receive lashes for this prohibition, because it is a prohibition that covers many matters (a "general prohibition", Hilchot Sanhedrin 18:3).
because it says "and he has defiled his consecrated head". This shows that the prohibition lies in the nazirite's own act (unlike the law of shaving, as above in halakhah 11).

for he delayed the nazirite period of purity and performed an act. Since he performed an act to defile himself, and cannot now count the days of nazirite status in purity, he has postponed and delayed his pure nazirite period, and therefore receives lashes.
Likewise, if he took the nazirite vow in a cemetery, he receives lashes also for "you shall not delay". Because his staying there counts as an act.
as we have explained. Above, halakhah 18.
he does not nullify even one day of his nazirite period. Although he violated one of the nazirite prohibitions, his nazirite status does not cease, and these days count toward his nazirite period.
enough to bend the tip to the root. A length sufficient to bend the end of the hair to its root on the head.
until he has overgrown hair. Hair that has not been cut for thirty days is defined as "overgrown" (Commentary to the Mishnah, Nazir 6:3).
all the fine details of nazirite status are upon him. He must be careful with all the laws of the nazirite.
he nullifies everything. He cancels all the nazirite days he has kept until now, and must count the nazirite period anew.
for it says "and the first days shall fall". The earlier days of nazirite status, before he became impure, are as if they fell away and are void.
on the day his nazirite days are completed. On the last day of his nazirite period.
after the day of completion etc.. On the day after the nazirite period is completed, when the nazirite brings his offerings (see above 4:1).
if the blood of one of the offerings was sprinkled for him. If the blood of one of the offerings he brings at the end of his nazirite period was sprinkled on the altar.
he nullifies nothing. Since the blood was sprinkled, his nazirite period is considered complete (below 8:2).
but he brings his other offerings of purity when he becomes pure. Because it is forbidden to offer the sacrifices of one impure through a corpse until he becomes pure (Hilchot Bi'at Mikdash 2:12).
for the nazirite period and everything attached to it has been completed. Both the day of completion and the day of bringing the offerings and the shaving next to it have passed.

but he completes them after he brings his offering. After he brings an offering for his impurity, he completes the nazirite period he began, and the first or second day is counted among the days of his nazirite period.
until there are first days. The word "days" in the plural is interpreted as two days, so only once two days of nazirite status have already passed can the days "fall" and nullify his nazirite period.
the nazirite vow takes effect on him. He must observe all the prohibitions and laws of the nazirite, but the days are not counted toward his nazirite period.
and if he became impure again. For even an impure nazirite is forbidden to add impurity upon impurity, and if he did so he receives lashes (as explained above 5:16-17).

until he is sprinkled on the third and seventh days and immerses on the seventh. Like any person impure through a corpse, who is sprinkled with the water of the red heifer on the third and seventh days of his impurity, and after the sprinkling on the seventh day immerses and becomes pure in the evening (Hilchot Parah 11:1).
he begins counting only from the eighth day onward. After he brings his offerings (below halakhah 12).

and he receives lashes for staying there; and if he was warned not to take the nazirite vow there, he does not shave his hair when he leaves. The commentators found Rambam's wording difficult and proposed amending it: "and he receives lashes for staying there. And if he was warned not to take the nazirite vow there, he receives lashes. And he does not shave his hair when he leaves" (Radbaz, and similarly Kesef Mishneh). Its meaning: if he took the vow and was warned not to stay, he receives lashes if he stayed. But if he was warned before he took the vow not to accept nazirite status, he receives lashes even if he did not stay. In any case, he does not shave his hair when he leaves, since the nazirite status has taken effect (and according to their explanation there is no disagreement between Ra'avad and Rambam on this law; see also Arukh HaShulchan 18:9, who amended and explained Rambam differently).

and if he became impure there in the cemetery with one of the impurities for which a nazirite shaves etc.. Since being in a cemetery he presumably became impure through a corpse, though not necessarily with an impurity for which a nazirite shaves (see below 7:1-6). And even if he became impure inside the cemetery with an impurity for which a nazirite shaves, he is not obligated to shave and bring an offering, because only one who vowed in purity and became impure brings an offering, unlike one who vowed in impurity, as explained in the halakhah above.
and he removed the covering from over him. He opened the cover.

even though he stayed there he does not receive lashes, but he is given rabbinic lashes for rebellion if he stayed. Because his impurity was not by his intent but by compulsion, he does not receive biblical lashes even if he was warned (unlike above 5:19, where one who entered a cemetery inadvertently receives lashes if warned, since his entry was forbidden even if done inadvertently - Mareh HaKorban).
those days do not count for him. They do not count toward his nazirite period, since he has not yet become pure of his impurity.

the days he counted count for him. Only when he became impure with an impurity for which the nazirite does not shave and does not bring an offering (for the details of the types of impurity see below 7:1-2); therefore this impurity does not nullify his nazirite period, and the days he spent outside the cemetery count for him. But if he became impure with an impurity for which the nazirite shaves and brings an offering, he nullifies, as stated below.

even if he entered on his eighth day, his seventh counts toward the tally. Since he took the vow in a cemetery, he does not bring an offering on the eighth day, and the seventh counts toward the nazirite count (as above, halakhah 7).
A nazirite who became impure with one of the impurities for which he shaves. Those detailed below 7:1-2.
like all those impure through a corpse. As explained in Hilchot Parah 11:1.
and waits for his sun to set. He waits until evening.
When does he begin counting. He renews his nazirite period.
as we have explained. Above, halakhah 12.

he need not shave at the entrance of the Temple, nor throw his hair on the fire. Unlike the shaving of purity, in which he shaves his hair in the Temple courtyard and throws it into the fire under the pot in which the peace offering is cooked (below 8:2-3).
in the country. Outside the Temple.
his hair is forbidden for benefit. As it says, "he shall be holy, letting the locks of the hair of his head grow long" (Numbers 6:5), and our Sages learned that his grown hair is holy.

and its ashes are forbidden like the ashes of everything that is buried. For all items forbidden for benefit that are buried, their ashes are forbidden for benefit (unlike forbidden items that are burned, whose ashes are permitted, Hilchot Pesulei HaMukdashin 19:13).

whether or not they warned him about each and every one. Although in such a case he receives lashes for each and every impurity (as above 5:16), he does not bring a separate offering for each impurity, but one offering for all.
who was delayed several days after his purification before bringing his sin offering. He was delayed and did not bring his offerings on the eighth day.
after he brought his sin offering, even though he has not yet brought his guilt offering and his burnt offering. For with the bringing of the sin offering he can already begin a pure nazirite period.
A nazirite who shaved the shaving of purity. After he completed his nazirite period properly.
if he became impure with a known impurity. An impurity that was known to someone.
and if he became impure with the impurity of the depths. As explained below, halakhah 18.
he does not nullify. And the nazirite period he completed stands.
a halakhah from the tradition. A tradition of the Sages.

and if, before the blood of one of the offerings was sprinkled for him, it became known that he was impure... he nullifies everything. Since before the sprinkling of the blood of one of the offerings, the earlier nazirite period had not been completed, even with the impurity of the depths he nullifies his nazirite period.

it became known to him after the blood of one was sprinkled. In this case the nazirite is already permitted to drink wine and to become impure (as below 8:5), and the earlier nazirite period has already ended.
only for a corpse. One who died naturally.
but not for one who was killed, for the one who killed him knew of him. And this is not defined as the impurity of the depths.
if it was found sunk in the bottom of a cave with water over it, it is the impurity of the depths. Because no human eye reaches there.
sunk in straw or in pebbles. Covered with straw, or with stones and dirt.
in water, in darkness, and in cracks of rocks. In these places it is not certain that no one ever saw it, since a human eye can reach there.
and he went down and immersed in the cave. On the seventh day after the sprinkling, he went down to immerse in a cave containing a spring of water.

because he was established as impure, and the presumption of an impure person is that he is impure until he is certainly purified. Since he was in a state of impurity, he does not leave his impurity until he is purified with certainty, and since there was a corpse in the cave, it turns out he did not leave his impurity, even though it is the impurity of the depths.
went down to cool off. A pure nazirite who went down into the water to cool his body.
he is pure until it becomes known that he touched. He remains in his presumption of purity.
the corpse was found floating on the surface of the water. And it is not known whether the nazirite touched it or not.

for which the nazirite does not shave and which do not nullify the previous days. He does not bring impurity offerings if he becomes impure through these impurities, and the nazirite days he kept are not cancelled.
with impurities that come from the body of the corpse itself. Parts of the body of the corpse whose quantity or form make them count as an entire corpse.
These are the impurities from a corpse for which a nazirite shaves. For further details on the laws of corpse impurity listed here, see Hilchot Tum'at Met chapters 2-4.
even if its limbs were not joined by sinews. Sinews had not formed in it (see also ibid. 2:1).
and for an olive-bulk of the flesh of the corpse. A quantity of an olive-bulk of the flesh of the corpse.
netzel. Explained in the next paragraph.
and for bones that are the majority of the count of bones. The numerical majority of the bones of the body, which is 125 in a man and 126 in a woman (ibid. 2:8-9).

and for bones that are the majority of the structure of the corpse. The structure of a person consists of the shins, the thighs, the ribs and the spine. A majority of the structure is, for example, two shins and one thigh (ibid.).

even if they do not contain a quarter-kav. A volume of about 300 cc. When they contain a quarter, it is impure even without a majority of the count or of the structure, but he does not shave (below halakhah 6).
the spine. The vertebral column.
that is on them. On the limb, from a dead or a living person.

flesh on which healing could grow in a living person. Even if some of the flesh on the limb is missing, if the flesh remaining on it could have healed had it been attached to a living person, it is considered like the bone of a corpse (Hilchot Tum'at Met 2:3-4).
half a log. A volume of about 150 cc.
the decay of a corpse. The dust remaining from the body of the corpse after its moisture has dried up and its bones have crumbled.
or was buried in its shroud or in a wooden or metal coffin. In these cases, parts that crumbled from the shroud or coffin are mixed into the decay of the corpse.
only for a corpse. For a person who died a natural death.
to exclude one who was killed, for his blood is missing. And this is not the decay of a whole body.
or if his hair or nails were cut and buried with him. After decomposition, the hair and nails are mixed into the decay.
he ground the corpse and left its dust until all of it decayed. That is, he did not grind it down to actual decay but only to dust, and it finished decaying after the grinding.
by tent. By the impurity of a tent, since with the impurity of touching or carrying he shaves even for a bone the size of a barley grain, as below, halakhah 6.

this is in doubt as to being impure. For with a quarter-log of bones that are not a majority of the structure or count, he becomes impure but does not shave (below halakhah 6), and because of the severity of the spine and skull, it is in doubt whether he shaves for a quarter of them.
for it is impossible to touch all of it, since it is not a single body. Rather, it is made up of separate crumbs.
the size of a barley grain. The volume of a grain of barley.
and a single bone does not convey impurity by tent. Even if its size is as large as a quarter-kav (Hilchot Tum'at Met 2:10).

he became impure through a clod of earth from a foreign land. The Sages decreed corpse impurity upon the soil of the lands of the nations, because they are not careful to bury in one place, and it is likely that the soil contains corpse bones the size of a barley grain (Hilchot Tum'at Met 2:16, Commentary to the Mishnah, Ohalot 2:3).

in a field in which a grave was plowed. A field in which there was a grave that was plowed, and now bones of a corpse are scattered throughout the field, and the Sages decreed corpse impurity upon it (called a "beit hapras", see Hilchot Tum'at Met 10:1).

or a tent was formed over him and over one of the twelve etc.. One of the types of tent described here was formed over the nazirite together with one of the twelve impurities listed above in halakhah 2.
the branches that extend from trees. Tree branches that shade the ground.

the projecting stones that extend from a fence. Stones that protrude from a fence and shade the ground. These tents are defined as a shaky tent and count as a tent only by rabbinic decree (Hilchot Tum'at Met 13:2).
a bed or a camel and the like. Tents made by a person, an animal or vessels bring impurity only by rabbinic decree (ibid. 19:6).

with a golel or a dofek. The golel is the cover placed on top of the grave, and the dofeks are the stones supporting the golel from the sides; they convey impurity by tent and by touch by rabbinic decree (ibid. 2:15).
that do not have flesh as required. Explained above in halakhah 2.
seven-day impurity. Seven days.
and is sprinkled on the third and seventh days. With the water of the red heifer, which purifies from corpse impurity.
touched the tent of the corpse or vessels that touched the corpse. His law is that he is impure with seven-day impurity (see Hilchot Tum'at Met 5:3, 5:12).
as will be explained in Hilchot Tum'at Met. 5:3-5.

so that the days of his impurity through vessels count toward the count of his nazirite days. So that these days be counted toward the count of his nazirite period, the law of a nazirite was made different from that of other people, and in this case he does not need sprinkling on the third and seventh days.
who became leprous and was confirmed. Who developed a leprous affliction and the priest declared him definitively impure (called a "confirmed leper").
all the days of his confirmation. The days during which he is a confirmed leper.

and the seven days of his counting, which he counts after he becomes pure of his leprosy between the first shaving and the second. After the affliction has healed and the priest purifies him, the leper shaves the first shaving and immerses, counts seven days, shaves the second shaving and immerses again (Hilchot Tum'at Tzara'at 11:1-2).
days of quarantine. When the priest does not declare the affliction definitively impure but quarantines it for seven days for a further examination (called a "quarantined leper").

Likewise, if a man or woman has a discharge from the flesh. Their law is that after the discharge stops they must wait seven days and immerse on the seventh and bring an offering on the eighth day (see Hilchot Mechusrei Kapparah 1:6, 3:1).

all the days of their discharge count for them even though they are impure. Because days of discharge do not require shaving (similar to the quarantine days of a leper), these days can count for the nazirite toward his count of nazirite days (see Babylonian Talmud, Nazir 56b).
with other impurities. Impurities lighter than that of a discharge, such as the impurity of a creeping creature or a carcass.
became impure through a corpse during the days of his leprosy. A nazirite who became leprous during his nazirite days, and during the days of his leprosy became impure through a corpse.
for he stands in his nazirite status even though he is impure. Although the days of his leprosy do not count toward his nazirite days, he is still considered a nazirite.
with the impurity of a met mitzvah. As explained below, halakhah 12.
and with the shaving of a mitzvah. As below, halakhah 15.
for it is a mitzvah for him to drink. Because of his oath.
for it is only rabbinic. Although the mitzvah of Kiddush is biblical, the obligation to recite Kiddush over wine is rabbinic (see Hilchot Shabbat 29:1, 29:6).
words of tradition. Halakhic tradition.

for his holiness is a temporary holiness, even if he was a lifelong nazirite. Even a lifelong nazirite's holiness is not an inherent holiness dependent on him from birth but arises from his acceptance of nazirite status, and he also has the possibility of annulling it, unlike priesthood (Lechem Mishneh; and see also Hilchot Evel 3:9).
they encountered him. A met mitzvah.
let a thirty-day nazirite become impure. Whose holiness is lighter than that of a hundred-day nazirite.

for the holiness of a lifelong nazirite is more severe than this. Although a lifelong nazirite shaves every twelve months, while a nazirite for a fixed time, even if he vowed for a thousand years, does not shave during his nazirite period (as above 3:12), the severity of a lifelong nazirite stems both from the fact that he must bring offerings with each shaving and from the fact that a fixed-time nazirite vow can be as short as thirty days (Radbaz).
he shaves all his hair. For the leper's shaving at the end of his leprosy.
wherever you find a positive and a negative commandment. That contradict each other (for this principle see also Hilchot Tzitzit 3:6, Hilchot Yibbum VeChalitzah 6:10).
as we have explained. Above, halakhah 9.

and the positive commandment is annulled by itself and only the negative commandment remains. It turns out that there is only the positive commandment of the leper's shaving versus the negative commandment of the nazirite's shaving, and the positive overrides the negative.

the shaving of purity. The process of ending the nazirite period of the nazirite, detailed in the Torah (Numbers 6:13-21), is called "the shaving of purity" after the shaving the nazirite does, although it also includes bringing offerings and other matters to be detailed in this chapter.
he brought all three and did not specify. He did not say explicitly which is for the sin offering, which for the burnt offering and which for the peace offering.

the one fit for a sin offering is offered as a sin offering, the one fit for a peace offering as a peace offering, and the one fit for a burnt offering as a burnt offering. The male lamb for the burnt offering, the ewe lamb for the sin offering, and the ram for the peace offering.
six tenths and two thirds of a tenth of fine flour. The isaron is a tenth of an ephah, with a volume of about 2.1 liters.
he bakes twenty loaves from them. It turns out that the size of each loaf is a third of an isaron.

ten loaves of matzot and ten wafers of matzot, and he anoints the twenty with a quarter-log of oil. The matzot are mixed with oil before baking while still flour, whereas the wafers are anointed with oil only after baking (Hilchot Ma'aseh HaKorbanot 9:21), and the total oil used to make the nazirite's bread is a quarter-log (see also ibid. 9:23).
and this measure is a law given to Moses at Sinai. The measure of a quarter-log of oil for anointing the matzot and wafers.
and he brings the twenty in one vessel. This vessel is called a basket (as below, halakhah 4), as in the verse: "the basket of matzot" (Numbers 6:17).

he cooks them. Boils them lightly in water without spices (see Commentary to the Mishnah, Berakhot 6:8 and the note of Rabbi Y. Kafih there; and so the commentator on Nazir 45b explained), and some explain that "shaluk" means thoroughly cooked (Tosafot and Rosh, Nazir there; and see Meiri, Nedarim 49a, that the word is interpreted in both senses, depending on the context).
the pot of the peace offerings. The cooking pot of the peace offering.
the cooked foreleg of the ram. The right front leg of the ram, which was cooked (Hilchot Ma'aseh HaKorbanot 9:10).

and he waves them. The priest puts his hand under the hand of the nazirite, man or woman, and waves the foreleg with the loaf and the wafer. Together with them they would wave the breast, the thigh and the sacrificial portions (ibid. 9:9).
a plucked nazirite. Whose head hairs were plucked out, or who is bald and has no hair.
who has no palms. And therefore cannot wave.

he drinks and becomes impure at evening. Some explain that this speaks of one who brought his offerings on the day his nazirite period ended, and so when he does not shave he must wait until the end of the day to drink or to become impure. But if he brought his offerings after that day, he may drink and become impure immediately after bringing the offerings (Orach Mishor; for further explanations see Radbaz, Or Sameach and R. Y. Kafih).
and he left two hairs, he did nothing. For as long as there are two hairs on his head, he is not considered shaved.
whether a pure nazirite or an impure nazirite. Whether with the shaving of purity described here or with the shaving of impurity described above, 6:11.

and his whole head grew back and he shaved it all again, with those two hairs. But if he shaved only the two hairs he left from the previous shaving and left the rest of the hair that grew, he did not fulfill the mitzvah of shaving (Kesef Mishneh and Radbaz; see Mareh HaKorban, who disagrees).
or he shaved one and one remained. When he had only two hairs on his head.

one fell out and he shaved one, there is no mitzvah of shaving here. Because when he shaved there were not two hairs on his head, and shaving a single hair is not defined as fulfilling the mitzvah of shaving. Therefore he must wait until two hairs grow and shave them.
he shaved on the peace offering. After the peace offering was offered, for example if they offered it first.
and it was found invalid. The offering was disqualified.
his shaving is invalid. For he shaved before bringing his offerings, and he is judged as one who shaved during his nazirite days, who must nullify thirty days and only then bring his offerings.
and his sacrifices did not count for him. Because he is considered as having offered during his nazirite days.

on the sin offering, and it was found that it was slaughtered not for the sake of a sin offering. And the sin offering is disqualified when slaughtered not for its own sake (Hilchot Ma'aseh HaKorbanot 4:11).

and they were slaughtered not for their own sake. Although the burnt offering and peace offering are not disqualified when slaughtered not for their own sake, they do not discharge the owner's obligation of the offering he owes but count as a freewill offering (Hilchot Ma'aseh HaKorbanot 4:10). And since this is so, it turns out he shaved before bringing his offerings.
and afterwards he brought other offerings to offer them for their own sake. After he shaved, he again brought the burnt offering and peace offering for the sake of the nazirite vow.
he shaved on all three and one of them was found valid, his shaving is valid. Because in the end he shaved on one of the offerings (see above, halakhah 2).
as we have explained. Above, 6:1.
not in accordance with their mitzvah. That he slaughtered them not for their sake (Hilchot Pesulei HaMukdashin 15:20).

and they are eaten for one day. Unlike freewill peace offerings, which are eaten for two days and one night, these peace offerings follow the law of the nazirite's peace offering, eaten for one day only, even though the nazirite did not discharge his obligation of bringing a peace offering by them.
and they do not require bread. The loaves that come with the nazirite's offering.

nor gifts. The commentators found this detail difficult, since every peace offering requires giving the breast and thigh to the priest (Lechem Mishneh; and see the commentators who explained in various ways, and Orach Mishor suggested emending Rambam's words here).
nor the foreleg. He does not need to give the priest the cooked foreleg of the ram.
all of it from unconsecrated funds, like other vows of dedication. A person cannot bring them with money of second tithe, only with money of unconsecrated produce.
as will be explained in its place. Hilchot Ma'aseh HaKorbanot 16:15.
he is a nazirite. Because when he said "I am a nazirite," he had already accepted nazirite status upon himself, so the condition he added afterward is meaningless.
and he set aside the unspecified money. Without dividing it into three portions and stating that each portion is for one of the nazirite's offerings.
the money falls to freewill offerings. It is given to the Temple and burnt offerings of the public are bought from it as freewill offerings (Hilchot Shekalim 2:2).
and the firstborn takes a double portion of it. According to the law of inheritance (Hilchot Nachalot 2:1).
a lifelong nazirite. Who shaves every twelve months.
a nazirite for a fixed time. Who does not shave during his nazirite period.

one who says, "It is incumbent on me to shave a nazirite". This speaks of a person who is not a nazirite and who by saying "It is incumbent on me to shave a nazirite" vowed to bring the offerings for another nazirite.
for he bound himself only to nazirite status. Because by saying "and I" he intended only to accept nazirite status and not to vow the offerings of another nazirite.
that he should offer from them the offerings of nazirites. That he should fund from them the offering of offerings for other nazirites.
and he offered from them and some remained. After he funded nazirite offerings from them, money was left over.
he should bring with the remainder the offerings of other nazirites. He should give it to other nazirites to fund their offerings (see also Hilchot Pesulei HaMukdashin 5:9).
unspecified money. See below, halakhah 4.
to a freewill offering. The money is given to the eleventh chest that was in the Temple, with which burnt offerings are bought as freewill offerings (see also Hilchot Shekalim 2:2).
and some remained. Money was left over after he finished offering his offerings.
shall go to a burnt offering. He offers a burnt offering with it.

and the surplus of the sin offering goes to the Dead Sea. To a place where the money is lost and cannot be of benefit (and "the Dead Sea" is the Great Sea - Hilchot Arachin VaCharamin 8:8 according to precise versions; and see Hilchot Shekalim 2:2, that a surplus of a sin offering is permitted for a freewill offering, and the commentators discussed the matter - see Tzafnat Pa'neach and Arukh HaShulchan 27:8).
and they do not require bread. He need not bring with them the loaves that come with the nazirite's offering.

and they are eaten for one day. Unlike ordinary peace offerings, which are eaten for two days and a night, these peace offerings are eaten for one day, as with the nazirite's peace offering (see Hilchot Ma'aseh HaKorbanot 10:6-7).
and he died. Before he managed to use this money to bring his offerings.

if they were unspecified they fall to freewill offerings. The law is that one who sets aside money for his sin offering and dies, the money goes to the Dead Sea (Hilchot Pesulei HaMukdashin 5:1). And although the nazirite's money includes sin offering money, it is a law given to Moses at Sinai that the unspecified money of a nazirite who died goes to freewill offerings (see Babylonian Talmud, Nazir 25b).
they are like specified. And we estimate from them the price of a sin offering and take it to the Dead Sea, and the rest is estimated for the burnt offering and peace offering.
a blemished animal. Which is unfit to be offered, and his intention was to sell it and use its proceeds.

even though he said, "This is for my sin offering, my burnt offering and my peace offering," it is like unspecified money. Because unlike money, a vessel is not divided into portions (Lechem Mishneh), and also because one does not buy with a vessel directly but first converts it into money (Ne'um David, and see other commentators who discussed the matter).

these are for my sin offering and the rest for my nazirite status. That he designated part of the money for the sin offering and the rest for the other offerings of the nazirite period, which are the burnt offering and the peace offering.
or she was a woman and her husband annulled it for her. That a woman who vowed to be a nazirite said so, and after her husband heard, he annulled her vow.
the value of the sin offering goes to the Dead Sea. Like one who set aside his sin offering and died (and as above, halakhah 3).
and the rest fall to freewill offerings. Like one who set aside unspecified money and died (above, halakhah 3).
they go out and graze with the flock. Like unconsecrated animals, and they have no holiness at all.
a dedication made in error. For he consecrated the animals in error.
as will be explained in its place. Hilchot Arachin 6:34.

if the animal was his. For example, he gave her ownership of his animals in general and told her that if she needs an animal for an offering she may take from his animals, for otherwise, even without his annulment, the animal would not have become consecrated (Tosafot, Nazir 24b), and when he annuls, he reveals his intention was not to transfer ownership to her for this purpose.
it goes out and grazes with the flock. And has no holiness.
for a person cannot consecrate something that is not his. See Hilchot Arachin VaCharamin 6:21.

for example, if it was given to her as a gift on condition that the husband have no authority over it etc.. For without this condition, everything in the woman's possession belongs to her husband (see Hilchot Zechiyah UMatanah 3:12, Hilchot Ishut 22:30).

the sin offering shall die. The Sage's uprooting uproots the vow entirely and therefore the animals go out to unconsecrated status, but with the husband's annulment there is no uprooting of the vow from its inception but only from the moment of annulment onward, and therefore holiness does take effect on the animals (Jerusalem Talmud, Nazir 4:4), except that because of the annulment there is no need for atonement now, and it becomes like a sin offering whose owners died or achieved atonement, whose law is that it dies (see Hilchot Pesulei HaMukdashin 4:1).
and they are eaten for one day and do not require bread. As above, halakhah 2.
she set it aside. From money belonging to her.
she set aside unspecified money etc.. As explained above, halakhot 3 and 4.

she brings an impurity offering. Because the husband does not uproot the vow from its inception but cancels it only from the moment of annulment onward, she is liable for an offering for her impurity.
a man who bound his son by a nazirite vow. As above, 2:13-14.
and he or a relative protested etc.. And by these actions his nazirite status did not take effect (above 2:15).
the sin offering shall die. Similar to the law of a husband annulling his wife's vow (above, halakhah 9).
he set aside unspecified money for him. The father set aside money for his son after he bound him by a nazirite vow.
and his wife miscarried. And at that stage he is not obligated in nazirite status (above 1:17).
and she conceived and gave birth again. And now he is obligated in nazirite status (ibid.).

the offerings are in doubt. Because he set them aside before she miscarried, we are in doubt whether his intention was to consecrate them only for the birth of the son with whom she was then pregnant, in which case the offerings are not consecrated, or whether he intended also for another son, in which case the offerings are consecrated.
and they are forbidden for shearing and work. Like doubtfully consecrated animals, which may not be sheared or worked (see Hilchot Me'ilah 1:8).
and they count the days of another complete nazirite period. Each one observes nazirite status for the number of days of the nazirite period he vowed in the earlier nazirite period.
after. After.
and they again bring an offering of purity. At the end of the second nazirite period.
it turns out they lost nothing in their offerings. For they brought one impurity offering and two purity offerings, as they would have brought even without the doubt.

one of them died. And the aforementioned condition cannot be carried out. And he cannot offer, on account of the doubt, the sin offering and guilt offering of impurity offerings and stipulate that they be freewill offerings, for these do not come as freewill offerings.

he brings a bird sin offering. For the doubtful impurity offering, and a bird sin offering comes for a doubt (Hilchot Shegagot 11:2), and the burnt offering and guilt offering do not hold him back from beginning to count another nazirite period (above 6:12).
and an animal burnt offering. For the doubtful shaving of purity, so that he can shave, and it suffices for a nazirite to have one offering in order to shave (above 8:5).
and he says, "If I was impure etc.". A similar condition appears in more detail below, 10:7.
offering of purity. Sin offering, burnt offering and peace offering (above 8:1).
and this is obligatory. And this animal burnt offering is obligatory.
and this is the rest of my offering. The sin offering and the peace offering.
and neither of the two. Of the two nazirites, one of whom became impure in doubt.
shaves the shaving of impurity. At the end of the first nazirite period.
unless they were minors or women. Who are not commanded concerning the prohibition of rounding the corners of the head (see Hilchot Avodah Zarah 12:1-3).

for these do not round the corners of their heads in doubt. And since each of them is in doubt whether he became impure, they do not shave the shaving of impurity but shave only once for their purity (see also below 10:9).
for a doubt of impurity there is impure. For in a private domain the Sages were stringent that a person who may have touched impurity there is impure (see Hilchot She'ar Avot HaTum'ot 15:8, 16:1).
as will be explained in its place. There.
in what case does this apply. That the nazirites are liable for an offering because of a doubtful impurity on the testimony of one witness.
as we have explained. Above, halakhah 16.

even though the basis of the nazirite status is through one witness. For the need for two witnesses for liability to lashes is only at the time of the act, but for establishing a prohibition, such as in our case the acceptance of nazirite status, two witnesses are not needed and one suffices (see Hilchot Sanhedrin 16:6).
but over him. And if the nazirite passes by it, he will become impure through a tent.
or touching its side. And through this touching he became impure.
even though it is a known impurity. To people, unlike the impurity of the depths (as above 6:18-19).

since a doubt in the public domain is pure. It is possible that he leaned but did not form a tent and did not touch (and specifically for a nazirite they were lenient even though it is nearly certain that he touched, whereas for terumah they were stringent in this doubt - see Hilchot She'ar Avot HaTum'ot 18:2-3; Lechem Mishneh).
and that he not move. That he not move the corpse even without direct touching. For one who moves a corpse becomes impure (Hilchot Tum'at Met 1:7).
laden. Carrying a load.
or riding. On an animal.

a person does not shave one shaving that counts for both his nazirite status and his leprosy. A nazirite shaves one shaving at the end of his nazirite days (above 8:1-4), and a leper shaves two shavings: one when he rises from the impurity of leprosy, and the second after seven days ("the days of his counting") at the end of his leprosy days (Hilchot Tum'at Tzara'at 11:1). And a person cannot shave one shaving that counts as both the nazirite shaving and the leprosy shaving, since they are essentially different matters.

and the shaving of leprosy, when he is a doubtful leper, does not override nazirite status. The shaving of a certain leprosy overrides the prohibition of shaving during nazirite status (above 7:15), but a doubtful leprosy does not override, and therefore he cannot shave for his doubtful leprosy during his nazirite days.
one who vowed nazirite status for one year. Accepted upon himself nazirite status for one year.
and at the end of the year became impure in doubt. In doubt of corpse impurity.
he counts seven days and is sprinkled on the third and seventh. Like the law of one purifying from corpse impurity (Hilchot Parah 11:1).
and does not shave on the seventh. The shaving of impurity that is normally practiced by a nazirite who became impure, but must perform the order of shavings explained shortly.
but only after four years. For only after four years does he come out of all his doubts and complete his nazirite period, as will be explained below.

and eats of sacred offerings after two years. For before that he had not finished the process of purification from his leprosy, as will be explained below, and he is defined as "lacking atonement", who is forbidden to eat sacred offerings (Hilchot Tum'at Tzara'at 11:2, Hilchot Mechusrei Kapparah 1:1; but a nazirite is permitted to eat sacred offerings even before finishing his purification process).
the shaving of purity. That the nazirite shaves at the end of his nazirite days.
and the shaving of impurity in doubt. That a nazirite shaves when he became impure through a corpse with an impurity for which the nazirite shaves (above 7:2).

after the first year. From when he vowed. And he does not shave earlier because of his doubtful impurity and leprosy, since he vowed nazirite status for a year and perhaps he did not become impure and was not a leper.
and he shaves with it his head, beard and eyebrows. As in the shaving of a leper, since the nazirite need only shave the hair of the head.
like other lepers. For the process of purification of the leper see Hilchot Tum'at Tzara'at 11:1.

and if he is neither impure through a corpse nor a leper, this is the shaving of purity of his nazirite status. For the nazirite is obligated to shave the hair of his head at the end of his nazirite period, and this shaving counts for his purity.
perhaps he is not a leper. For if he were certainly a leper, his shaving would override nazirite status, but since there is doubt, it does not override.

and this second year he is a nazirite in it. For if he had indeed been impure through a corpse in the first year, his first shaving was a shaving of impurity, and since a nazirite who became impure during his nazirite days, whether with certain impurity or doubtful impurity, nullifies his nazirite days (above 6:3), he must now begin counting nazirite status anew for a year and is forbidden to shave until the end of the year.
the purification from leprosy was completed. For he is obligated in two shavings for his purification.

and the first year did not count for him because it is the days of his confirmation. The days in which he was a definitive leper, and the days of confirmation of a leper do not count toward his nazirite days (above 7:9).
and the second year did not count for him because it is the days of the leper's counting. And the days of the leper's counting also do not count toward his nazirite days (ibid.).
and none of the three years counts. Toward the obligation of nazirite status.
and he shaves the fourth shaving. And after this shaving he has certainly completed his nazirite period.

and his hair in every doubtful shaving is forbidden for benefit in doubt. For the hair of a nazirite, both in the shaving of purity and in the shaving of impurity, is forbidden for benefit (above 6:14, 8:2; and see also Hilchot Pesulei HaMukdashin 19:10-11). And since each of these four shavings is a doubtful shaving of a nazirite, the hair is forbidden in doubt.

the hair of a nazirite who became leprous is permitted for benefit. Unlike the shavings mentioned here, which are doubtful shavings of a nazirite for his impurity or his purity, the hair of a leper's shaving is permitted even if he is a nazirite.
the first shaving for the doubt of the days of his leprosy. Perhaps he was a leper and the leprosy shaving precedes the nazirite shavings.

if he was rich he writes his property over to others. A rich leper who has become pure brings a lamb for a guilt offering, a lamb for a burnt offering and a ewe lamb for a sin offering, and a poor leper brings a lamb for a guilt offering and two turtledoves or two young pigeons, one for a burnt offering and one for a sin offering (Hilchot Shegagot 10:3, Hilchot Mechusrei Kapparah 1:3). And since he is a doubtful leper he cannot bring a ewe lamb as a sin offering, because an animal sin offering is not offered for a doubt, and so he must give his property as a gift to others so that he becomes poor and can bring a bird sin offering, which can be brought for a doubt.
and afterwards he brings a bird sin offering and an animal burnt offering etc.. As will be detailed in the following halakhot.

and none of the bird sin offerings among them is eaten because it is in doubt. Perhaps he is a pure nazirite and is not liable for the bird sin offering. And a bird sin offering that comes for a doubt is not eaten (Hilchot Pesulei HaMukdashin 7:10).
as we have explained. Above, 8:1.
for the doubt of his impurity. Perhaps he is an impure nazirite whose sin offering holds him back from beginning to count a pure nazirite period (above 6:12).

the second for the doubt of his leprosy, for a leper brings his offering only after the second shaving. It turns out that the first sin offering was only for the doubt of his impurity, and this one only for the doubt of his leprosy, for if he became impure, he was already purified by the previous sin offering.
and likewise the third sin offering is for the doubt of his impurity. And not for the doubt of his leprosy, for if he was a leper he already fulfilled his obligation with the two previous shavings.
as we have explained. Above, halakhah 2.
that he brings with them. That he brings together with the sin offerings at the first, second and third shaving.

if I am pure, this is from my obligation. For in order to shave the nazirite must bring an offering (and although he must also bring an animal sin offering and a peace offering, he may shave on the burnt offering alone, as above 8:2).

and if I am impure, it is a freewill offering. For a nazirite who became impure does not bring an animal burnt offering but a bird burnt offering (and the shaving of impurity will be performed on the bird sin offering that he brought).

and so he says for the second and third. For in each of them it is possible that he is a pure nazirite and must bring a burnt offering in order to shave on it for his purity, and it is possible that he is impure (through corpse impurity or through his leprosy) and this burnt offering is a freewill offering.
and he brings the offering of purity in the fourth shaving. The three offerings of the shaving of purity: sin offering, burnt offering and peace offering.
and he stipulates and says etc.. The commentators had great difficulty with Rambam's details of the conditions in halakhot 7-8; below we point to some of the difficulties here.

If I was impure... and if I was confirmed. The commentators discussed whether the phrase "if I was impure" means that he was only impure or that he was at the same time a leper, and similarly they were uncertain regarding the statement "if I was confirmed" (see Kesef Mishneh, Radbaz, Mirkevet HaMishneh and others).

the first burnt offering is the obligation of a leper. Here too the commentators found it difficult that Rambam mentions the leper's burnt offering obligation at the fourth shaving, and they challenged this from several angles (see Ra'avad, Kesef Mishneh, Lechem Mishneh and others).

one for the obligation of a leper and one for the obligation of nazirite status. The first burnt offering for his leprosy and the second for his nazirite status. And here too the commentators asked how he brings his nazirite offering before counting the nazirite days (see Lechem Mishneh and Mirkevet HaMishneh).
and the third and fourth are freewill offerings. For he has already offered the obligation of his leprosy and the obligation of his nazirite status.
